section.title: The Ascension
section.sectionRationale: Luke opens his second volume by tying it to the first. The risen Jesus, proved alive by many convincing proofs, spends forty days teaching about the kingdom of God, then commissions the apostles, promises the Holy Spirit, and is taken up into heaven while two angels pledge His return. This is the launching point of the whole book: the ascended Christ pours out the Spirit and sends the gospel out from Jerusalem.
section.thesis: The ascended Christ, having shown Himself alive, commissions His church to be His witnesses in the power of the coming Spirit, from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth, and will return as surely and visibly as He departed.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the prologue linking Acts to Luke's Gospel and the forty days of resurrection teaching; the promise of the Spirit and the commission to the ends of the earth; and the ascension itself with the angels' promise that Jesus will come back.

units.label: The prologue and the forty days
units.note: all that Jesus began to do and to teach

verses.text: In my first book, O Theophilus, I wrote about all that Jesus began to do and to teach,
until the day He was taken up to heaven, after giving instructions through the Holy Spirit to the apostles He had chosen.
After His suffering, He presented Himself to them with many convincing proofs that He was alive. He appeared to them over a span of forty days and spoke about the {{basileia|kingdom}} of God.
And while they were gathered together, He commanded them: “Do not leave Jerusalem, but wait for the gift the Father promised, which you have heard Me discuss.
For John baptized with water, but in a few days you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.”

units.label: The promise of the Spirit and the commission
units.note: you will be My witnesses to the ends of the earth

verses.text: So when they came together, they asked Him, “Lord, will You at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?”
Jesus replied, “It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by His own authority.
But you will receive {{dynamis|power}} when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be My {{martys|witnesses}} in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.”

units.label: The ascension and the angels' promise
units.note: this same Jesus will come back

verses.text: After He had said this, they watched as He was {{analambano|taken up}}, and a cloud hid Him from their sight.
They were looking intently into the sky as He was going, when suddenly two men dressed in white stood beside them.
“Men of Galilee,” they said, “why do you stand here looking into the sky? This same Jesus, who has been taken from you into heaven, will come back in the same way you have seen Him go into heaven.”

basileia.gloss: Kingdom, reign, royal rule. The risen Jesus spends forty days teaching about the kingdom of God, His saving reign. The disciples still imagine a restored national kingdom for Israel, but the kingdom Jesus proclaims will advance through the Spirit and the witness of the church to all nations.

dynamis.gloss: Power, might, effective force. The apostles are not to launch the mission by their own strength but to wait for the power that comes when the Holy Spirit comes upon them. The same word describes the mighty works of God; here it is the enabling power for witness.

martys.gloss: Witness, one who testifies to what he has seen and knows. The apostles are eyewitnesses of the risen Christ, and their whole task is to testify to Him. From this word comes martyr, for many sealed their testimony with their lives.

analambano.gloss: To take up, lift up, receive up. Luke uses it for the ascension: Jesus was taken up into heaven. It marks His exaltation to the Father's right hand, from where He pours out the Spirit and reigns until He returns in the same way.

basic.context: Acts is the second volume Luke wrote for Theophilus. It picks up where the Gospel ended: the risen Jesus, before He returns to the Father, gives His final instructions. For forty days He proves He is truly alive and teaches about the kingdom of God. Then He tells the apostles to wait in Jerusalem for the Holy Spirit, commissions them as His witnesses, and is taken up into heaven.
basic.hermeneutics: This passage is the hinge between the Gospels and the mission of the church. Read verse 8 as the table of contents for the whole book: Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, and the ends of the earth. The key questions are: what did the ascension accomplish, what are the disciples to do while they wait, and what does it mean that Jesus will come back the same way He left?
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus promises dynamis, power, that comes only when the Holy Spirit arrives, so the apostles can be His martys, witnesses. He was analambano, taken up, into heaven, exalted to reign. And He keeps redirecting them from a merely national basileia, kingdom, to the worldwide reign that the gospel will spread.
basic.typology: The ascension answers the exaltation of the Son of Man in Daniel 7, who is given dominion over all peoples. Jesus goes up in a cloud, as the glory of God filled the tabernacle and temple, marking Him as the enthroned King. Elijah was taken up and his mantle fell on Elisha; here Jesus is taken up and the Spirit falls on His church.
basic.christ: This is Christ's coronation. Having suffered and risen, He is taken to the right hand of the Father, from where He pours out the Spirit and rules the world through His witnessing church. He is not absent but enthroned, and He will return visibly and personally, as truly as He departed.
basic.god: The Father governs the times and seasons by His own authority. He keeps His promise to send the Spirit. The whole mission is God's initiative, powered by God's Spirit, directed by God's plan, so that the church acts not on its own strength but on His.
basic.crossReferences: Luke 24 ends with the same ascension and the promise of power from on high. Daniel 7 shows the Son of Man given an everlasting dominion. Matthew 28 gives the great commission to all nations. Acts 2 shows the promised Spirit poured out at Pentecost.
basic.oneStory: The ascension is the turning point from what Jesus began to do and teach to what He continues to do through His Spirit and His church. The King is enthroned, the mission is launched, and the story runs from an upper room in Jerusalem to the ends of the earth, until the same Jesus returns.

context.literary:
The opening sentence of Acts is a deliberate hinge. 'In my first book, O Theophilus,' Luke recalls the opening of his Gospel, Luke 1:3, and then summarises that book as 'all that Jesus began to do and to teach.' The word 'began' matters. If the Gospel recorded what Jesus began, Acts records what He continues, now from heaven and through His people. Luke's two volumes are therefore one work in two panels, joined by the ascension, which closes the Gospel, Luke 24:50 to 53, and opens Acts.

Verses 1 to 5 are a compact prologue in the manner of a formal ancient preface, and the first paragraph is organised around two poles, the instruction Jesus gave and the apostles He gave it to. Verses 6 to 8 are a question and an answer. The apostles ask about the kingdom, and Jesus replies with a correction about timing and a promise about power. Verses 9 to 11 are a brief narrative of the departure and a speech by two angels.

The conversation in verses 6 to 8 is the spine of the passage. Verse 8 is not only a promise but an outline of the book: 'in Jerusalem' fills chapters 1 to 7, 'in all Judea and Samaria' chapters 8 to 12, and 'to the ends of the earth' the rest, ending in Rome. The book closes with Paul proclaiming 'the kingdom of God' in Rome, Acts 28:31, and the word 'kingdom' thus brackets the whole work, with the first and last pages speaking of it.

The angelic question, 'why do you stand here looking into the sky?' is a mild rebuke that turns the disciples around. They are told to look neither at the sky nor at the calendar, but to return to the city to wait and then to go out in witness.
context.historical:
Luke addresses a person named Theophilus, whose name means 'friend of God' and who is called 'most excellent' in Luke 1:3, a form of address suited to a person of some standing. Whether he was a patron, a believer or a Roman official is not known. Ancient books were written on scrolls of limited length, and Luke and Acts together are about a quarter of the New Testament, each volume filling roughly one scroll of the largest usable size.

The disciples' question about restoring 'the kingdom to Israel' arose from a long hope. Israel under Roman rule looked back to the throne of David and to prophecy that God would restore His people, Isaiah 1:26, Amos 9:11, Jeremiah 23:5 to 8. The apostles had lived three years with the one they believed to be Messiah. They had seen Him crucified and risen, and the natural conclusion was that the moment had come. Jesus does not deny the hope; He changes the order of events.

The Mount of Olives is the setting. It stands east of Jerusalem across the Kidron valley, and Acts 1:12 says it is 'a Sabbath day's journey away,' and the BSB footnote gives about three thousand feet, the distance that tradition allowed on the Sabbath. The mountain had its own associations. According to Ezekiel 11:23 the glory of the LORD left the city and stood on the mountain east of it, and Zechariah 14:4 pictured the LORD's feet standing on the Mount of Olives. For a Jewish ear, that ridge was where God's presence departs and returns.

The forty days are measured in the Old Testament scale, since forty is the number for testing and preparation in Moses' time on the mountain, Exodus 24:18, and Israel's years in the wilderness. The apostles are also being told to wait until Pentecost, which fell fifty days after Passover, Leviticus 23:15 and 16, so the days they spend waiting in Jerusalem fall within the pilgrim feast when the city was crowded with visitors from many nations.
context.canonical:
The ascension is the point where two lines of the Old Testament come together. The first is Daniel 7:13 and 14, where 'One like the Son of Man' comes with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days and receives dominion over every nation. The second is Psalm 110:1, 'Sit at My right hand,' which Peter will quote on the day of Pentecost, Acts 2:33 to 36. Together they say that the man Jesus has been given universal rule, and that the rule is exercised from heaven, not on the earth only.

The Gospel of Luke ends with the ascension, and Luke 24:49 is the promise of power that Acts 1:8 echoes. Matthew ends with the commission to all nations, Matthew 28:18 to 20, and John with the Spirit's coming promised in the farewell, John 14:16 and 16:7. Paul's letters take the ascension as the ground of Christ's headship, Ephesians 1:20 to 23 and 4:8 to 10, and Philippians 2:9 to 11 says God exalted Him to the highest place. Hebrews builds a doctrine on it: the Son has passed through the heavens and sits at the right hand, Hebrews 4:14 and 9:24.

The promise of the angels, that He will return in the same way, is picked up by Acts 3:20 and 21, 1 Thessalonians 4:16 and 17, and Revelation 1:7, which says 'Behold, He is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see Him.' The sequence of Luke 24, Acts 1 and Revelation 1 makes the ascension the middle of the story between the cross and the coming.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke wrote to give Theophilus certainty, Luke 1:4, and Acts continues that purpose. The ascension passage shows him establishing three things for his reader. First, continuity: the same Jesus who taught the Twelve is the one who now acts through them, and the same Spirit who anointed Him, Luke 4:18, now empowers them. Second, certainty about His resurrection: the 'many convincing proofs' and forty days of appearances are Luke's way of saying that what follows rests on firm ground, not rumour or vision. Third, the reorientation of the church's attention. The apostles ask for a kingdom restored to a nation, and Luke records that they were given a mission to the nations instead.

Luke does not want the reader to think of the ascension as a loss. The disciples return to Jerusalem 'with great joy,' Luke 24:52, and the angels' words in Acts 1:11 turn their gaze from the sky to the road ahead. The Lord who has been taken out of their sight has not been taken out of their story.

In writing this, Luke also gives the church its own sense of time. The time between the ascension and the return is not a gap to be filled with speculation about dates, verse 7, but an age in which witness is to be given in the power of the Spirit.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The ascension is a one time event. No later believer will see a cloud take Jesus up, and the apostles' role as eyewitnesses of the risen Lord is not repeated. What the passage prescribes for all believers is the pattern that follows from it: wait on God's promise, be His witnesses in every place, and live in hope of His return. The command to wait in Jerusalem, verse 4, was specific to that moment, since the Spirit was promised and given at Pentecost, but it teaches that mission begins with dependence.

Verse 7 is often applied as a rule for believers. 'It is not for you to know times or seasons' is directed to the apostles in answer to a question about the kingdom's timing. It is a fair application for the church that attempts to calculate dates for the end, but it does not forbid studying prophecy. The text is aimed at the idle curiosity of the question, not at faithful study.

The promise in verse 8, 'you will receive power,' is addressed to the apostles first and then, as Acts shows, to all believers, Acts 2:17 and 2:39. The geography of the verse describes the book's progress, but the command to be witnesses is not tied to a particular region.

debates.question: Was the apostles' question about the kingdom wrong?

views.label: It was mistaken in its expectations
views.case: Jesus answers by saying they do not need to know the times, and by redirecting them to mission. Some see a reproof of nationalistic hopes, since the apostles asked about 'the kingdom to Israel' and Jesus spoke of the 'ends of the earth.'

views.label: It was a right question asked at the wrong time
views.case: Jesus does not say the kingdom will not be restored. He says its timing belongs to the Father. Peter will later speak of 'the restoration of all things,' Acts 3:21, and Paul of Israel's future salvation, Romans 11:25 to 27. On this view the hope was right and the order was incomplete.

views.label: The question was answered in a new way
views.case: Another reading holds that the kingdom is being restored in Christ's enthronement and the Spirit's coming, and the rest of Acts reads Davidic promises as fulfilled in Jesus, Acts 2:30 to 36 and 15:16 to 18. Israel's restoration is happening in the gathering of Jew and Gentile around the risen king.

debates.bearing: All three agree that Jesus did not rebuke the hope itself, only the impulse to know the timetable, and all three agree the immediate task is witness. The verse leaves room for both a present and a future dimension of the kingdom.

debates.question: How should we understand 'in the same way' in verse 11?

views.label: A visible, personal, bodily return
views.case: The angels say this same Jesus will come back 'in the same way you have seen Him go.' He went visibly, bodily and with a cloud, and the return is described by Revelation 1:7 as seen by every eye. The mention of the Mount of Olives in verse 12 also fits Zechariah 14:4.

views.label: A certain return without precise detail
views.case: Some stress certainty over mode. The point of the angels' words is that the departure is not the end, and that the same person returns, not a replacement. The 'cloud' belongs to the biblical language of divine presence and judgement, Daniel 7:13, and need not be read as meteorology.

debates.bearing: Both views hold that the return is personal and certain, and both resist the idea that Jesus' ascension severed His connection with the world. They differ on how much detail the phrase carries.

study.originalLanguages:
The 'many convincing proofs' of verse 3 translate a single Greek noun, tekmerion, which means a sure sign or demonstration, and which occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. It is a word from the language of argument and evidence, and Luke's choice shows that the resurrection appearances are meant to be taken as demonstration, not as private visions. The appearance language fits: the risen Jesus ate with them, Luke 24:41 to 43 and Acts 10:41.

The verb in verse 4 that the BSB renders 'while they were gathered together' is given a second possibility in the footnote: 'Or eating together.' The Greek verb, sunalizo, was understood by some ancient readers as 'sharing salt,' that is, eating at table. The ambiguity is instructive. Either it was a gathering of the apostles, or it was a meal, and Luke's other accounts of the forty days include meals.

The apostles ask whether He will 'restore' the kingdom, using the verb apokathistemi. It is a word for setting something back to its original state, and it is used in the Gospels of healing, as a withered hand being restored, Matthew 12:13. In Acts 3:21 Peter uses the noun form of the same family for 'the restoration of all things.' Luke therefore uses the vocabulary of restoration for Israel's hope, and the answer in verse 8 does not dismiss it but sets it inside a larger plan.

Jesus says it is not for them to know 'times or seasons,' chronous e kairous. The pair appears in Daniel 2:21, where God 'changes the times and seasons' and again in 1 Thessalonians 5:1. Kairos is the appointed moment; chronos the span of time. The Father has fixed them 'by His own authority,' exousia, a word for right and power to decide. The statement places the calendar of history in the Father's hands.

In verse 8 the Spirit brings 'power,' dynamis, and makes the apostles martyres, witnesses. The word 'witness' in Acts moves from a legal sense of someone who has seen, Acts 1:22, to the later sense of someone who suffers for the testimony, from which the English word martyr is derived. That later sense is not yet in view in verse 8, but Luke's story will show how the first sense leads to the second. The phrase 'ends of the earth' comes from Isaiah 49:6, and Paul explicitly applies it to the mission in Acts 13:47.

Luke uses two verbs for the departure. In verse 9 the cloud scene uses epairo, 'lifted up,' and in verses 2, 11 and 22 he uses analambano, 'taken up.' The second is the verb the Greek Old Testament uses of Elijah in 2 Kings 2:11. Luke thus applies the vocabulary of Elijah's rapture to Jesus, while differing in what follows: Elijah leaves a mantle, and Jesus leaves a promise of the Spirit.

typology.type: The Son of Man coming with the clouds, Daniel 7:13 and 14
typology.fulfillment: Daniel sees one like a son of man approach the Ancient of Days on the clouds and receive dominion that will not pass away. At the ascension Jesus is taken up in a cloud, verse 9, and the angels say He will return the same way, verse 11. The vision is fulfilled in Jesus' entrance into the Father's presence and His enthronement, which Peter explains in Acts 2:33. The correspondence is closest at the cloud and the glory, and it escalates, since the dominion Daniel saw is exercised now through the Spirit and the church. The type is not exhausted, because the final public coming with the clouds, Revelation 1:7, still lies ahead.

typology.type: Elijah taken up and the mantle passed on
typology.fulfillment: Elijah went up into heaven, 2 Kings 2:11, and Elisha received a double portion of his spirit and carried on his work, 2 Kings 2:9 and 13. Luke uses the same verb of Jesus' ascension, analambano, and the disciples are left to continue the work with the Spirit. The correspondence is real, but the escalation is large. Elijah's successor received a portion of a prophet's spirit, whereas the disciples receive the Spirit of the Lord Himself, sent by the ascended Christ, Acts 2:33. The type falls short because Elijah's going left a prophet's work to be continued, while Christ's ascension is a coronation from which the nations are claimed.

typology.type: The cloud of glory over tabernacle and temple
typology.fulfillment: A cloud covered the Tent of Meeting and the glory of the LORD filled it, Exodus 40:34 and 35, and the cloud filled Solomon's temple, 1 Kings 8:10 and 11. The same cloud was at the transfiguration, Luke 9:34. In Acts 1:9 a cloud receives Jesus, which signals that He enters the realm of God's own presence. The point is not that He is lost in mist but that the glory-cloud that once marked God's dwelling now surrounds the risen man. The type falls short in that the cloud once settled on a building and now rests on a person who is Himself the temple, John 2:21.

typology.type: Moses' forty days and the prophet to come
typology.fulfillment: Moses spent forty days on the mountain receiving the law, Exodus 24:18, and Jesus spends forty days teaching about the kingdom after His resurrection. The parallel is one of pattern and not stated by Luke. Moses came down with the word for a people at Sinai; Jesus goes up leaving a promise that the Spirit will write the word within, Jeremiah 31:33 and Ezekiel 36:27. Pentecost, fifty days after Passover as Sinai was fifty days after the exodus by one common reckoning, gives the new covenant its answer to the old. The correspondence is suggestive but should be held lightly, since Luke does not make it himself.

study.christ:
The ascension is Christ's enthronement. Luke's Gospel ended with the Lord blessing His disciples as He was carried up, and Acts begins by showing what that exaltation means. Peter's first sermon draws the line plainly: Jesus has been 'exalted to the right hand of God' and has 'received from the Father the promised Holy Spirit and has poured out what you now see and hear,' Acts 2:33. The same man who died as a criminal reigns as Lord and Christ, Acts 2:36. The ascension means the cross was not defeat and the resurrection was not a mere return to the earlier life.

It also shows that the risen Christ is truly a man. He ascends in the body that was raised, which is why the early church confessed that human nature is now seated in heaven. Hebrews finds comfort in this: a high priest who has passed through the heavens and can sympathise with our weakness, Hebrews 4:14 and 15. He intercedes, Hebrews 7:25, and He prepares a place for us, John 14:2 and 3. The ascension is therefore not an absence but a ministry.

The ascension is also the beginning of His work through the Spirit. Luke says the Gospel was about what Jesus began to do and teach, verse 1, so Acts is about what He goes on doing. The risen Lord directs the mission. He speaks to Saul on the road, Acts 9:5, appears to Paul in the night, Acts 18:9 and 10. Luke even calls the Spirit who guides the mission 'the Spirit of Jesus,' Acts 16:7.

Finally, the ascension anchors hope in a promise. The angels say 'This same Jesus' will return, verse 11. The one coming is the same person with the same scars, the same voice and the same love for His friends. Guard against reading the passage as a simple allegory of heaven as 'up.' The cloud and the direction are the language of exaltation and presence, and what matters is that He is where the Father is, and that He will come again.
study.god:
This passage shows God as the one who keeps and fixes. The Father has 'fixed' times and seasons 'by His own authority,' verse 7, and what He has promised, He sends, verses 4 and 5. The sequence is all of grace. The apostles do nothing to earn the Spirit; they are told to wait for a gift. The God of Acts 1 is the one who takes the initiative in history and then invites His people into it.

The passage also helps us understand the Trinity in action. The Father promises, the Son commands through the Spirit, verse 2, and the Spirit comes to empower witness. Luke is careful to say that Jesus gave His instructions 'through the Holy Spirit' even before the ascension. The Son who is ascending is the same one who was anointed by the Spirit at His baptism and who acts through the Spirit now, as Acts will show.

God's patience and His sovereignty are held together. The disciples' impatient question is not met with sharpness. It is answered with a clear boundary and a better promise. God does not explain all of His calendar, but He does tell His people what to do in the meantime. This is typical of the way He speaks in Scripture: Deuteronomy 29:29 says that the secret things belong to the LORD and the revealed things belong to us.

For worship, the passage says that God's people are gathered by promise, not by sight. They do not see the Lord now. They are told to wait, to pray and to witness. The ascended Christ and the God who fixes times are the same God who is with His people, and the promise of power is a promise that they will not carry out His work by themselves. Worship in this light is trust in a God who is both enthroned and near, who is above all times and seasons, and who comes by His Spirit to those who wait.

crossReferences.note: Luke's Gospel ends with the same ascension, with the same promise of power from on high and the same command to wait in the city. Comparing the two accounts shows that Luke 24 gives the worship and joy of the disciples, and Acts 1 gives the commission and the angels' promise.

The Son of Man comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days and receives everlasting dominion over all peoples. Jesus often used the title, and at His trial He linked it to the right hand and the clouds, Mark 14:62. The ascension is the moment this vision begins to be fulfilled, with the cloud as the sign of entry into God's presence.

The LORD tells David's Lord to sit at His right hand until His enemies are made a footstool. Peter quotes it in Acts 2:34 and 35 to explain the ascension, so the text stands behind the whole book as the account of why Jesus is now reigning and why the mission advances.

Elijah is taken up and Elisha, who watched him go, receives the prophet's spirit and mantle. The story shows what it means to see the departure of one's master and then to be empowered. Acts 1 repeats the scene with a greater master and a greater gift.

The Servant is called to be a light to the nations so that God's salvation may reach the ends of the earth. The words of Acts 1:8 echo this, and Paul explicitly quotes Isaiah 49:6 in Acts 13:47. The mission of the church is the mission of the Servant carried on through His people.

The risen Lord claims all authority and sends His disciples to all nations, promising to be with them always. Acts 1:8 is the same commission in Luke's account, with the Spirit as the means of the promised presence and with a geographical outline of how the mission will unfold.

Ten days later the promise of verses 4 and 5 is fulfilled at Pentecost, when the Spirit fills the waiting believers. The reader of Acts 1 is meant to move straight to Acts 2, and the waiting of chapter 1 becomes the power of chapter 2.

The glory of the LORD leaves the city and stops on the mountain east of it, and later the prophet sees it come back from the east, Ezekiel 43:2 to 5. Jesus leaves from that same mountain, and the passage invites the reader to see His departure as the glory moving on, not vanishing, until it returns.

The LORD's feet will stand on the Mount of Olives on the day He comes to rescue His people. The angels' promise that this same Jesus will return, given at the Mount of Olives, links His return to this prophecy and suggests that the place of departure is the place of return.

Since we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, we can approach the throne of grace with confidence. The ascension is the foundation of this encouragement, because the Jesus who left in a cloud is the one who now represents His people before the Father.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story begins with God placing humanity in a garden as His image bearers to rule creation, Genesis 1:26 to 28, and the fall turns that rule to ruin. The promised seed, the covenant with Abraham, the kingdom of David and the hopes of the prophets all look for a man who will take the dominion that Adam lost. Daniel's vision is the summit of that hope: a human figure given everlasting dominion over every nation. The ascension is where that happens. A man, truly and bodily, is crowned.

The passage also answers the question left by the Gospels: what does the risen Jesus do next? He does not stay on earth to reign from Jerusalem, and He does not vanish from the story. He rises to the Father's right hand, pours out the Spirit, and sends His people out as His witnesses to every nation. This is the answer to the promise made to Abraham that all nations would be blessed, Genesis 12:3, and to the commission given to Israel to be a light to the nations, Isaiah 42:6 and 49:6, which Israel's own story had not yet carried out.

Looking forward, Acts 1 sets up everything that follows: Pentecost, the spread of the gospel across the Roman world, the gathering of Jews and Gentiles in one body. And it leaves the last act in the angels' promise. The ascension is not the end, because 'this same Jesus' will come. The final chapters of Scripture take up that promise: the Lamb is on the throne, the nations walk by His light, and the one who ascended from the Mount of Olives returns, Revelation 21:24 and 22:1 to 5. The new creation is the kingdom restored, in the way and at the time the Father has fixed.

quiz.q: What did Jesus tell the apostles to do before beginning their mission?

options.text: Wait in Jerusalem for the promised Holy Spirit and the power He brings.
options.note: Jesus commanded them to wait for the gift the Father promised before they went out.

options.text: Go at once to preach to all nations in their own strength.
options.note: They were commissioned to the nations, but first they had to wait for the Spirit's power, not act on their own strength.

options.text: Stay together in prayer while they waited for the Spirit.
options.note: True and part of the picture, but the explicit command was to wait in Jerusalem for the Spirit Jesus promised.

options.text: Set up an earthly kingdom to restore Israel's political power.
options.note: Jesus turned them away from this expectation; the kingdom would advance by the Spirit and witness, not political restoration.

quiz.q: What does Acts 1:8 map out for the church's mission?

options.text: Spirit-empowered witness to Christ, from Jerusalem to Judea and Samaria to the ends of the earth.
options.note: This is the programmatic verse and the outline of the whole book.

options.text: Witness beginning in Jerusalem and spreading outward from there.
options.note: Correct as far as it goes, but it omits the Spirit's power and the reach to the ends of the earth.

options.text: A call to perform signs and wonders to impress the crowds.
options.note: Signs accompany the mission at points, but the commission is to witness to Christ in the Spirit's power, not to perform wonders.

options.text: A promise that the disciples would rule Israel from Jerusalem.
options.note: Jesus explicitly redirected them away from a national kingdom to worldwide witness.

quiz.q: What does the ascension tell us about who Jesus now is?

options.text: He is exalted and enthroned, reigning from the Father's right hand and pouring out the Spirit.
options.note: The ascension is Christ's coronation; He now reigns and sends the Spirit.

options.text: He has simply gone away and left the church on its own.
options.note: The opposite is true: He is enthroned and active by His Spirit, and He will return.

options.text: He has returned to heaven to prepare to come back one day.
options.note: He will indeed return, but this understates that He is reigning now, not merely waiting.

options.text: He is a great teacher whose example the disciples must now follow.
options.note: He is more than an example to imitate; He is the enthroned Lord who empowers and directs His church.

quiz.q: What did the two men in white promise about Jesus?

options.text: This same Jesus will come back in the same way they saw Him go into heaven.
options.note: The angels promise a personal, visible return, matching His visible departure.

options.text: Jesus would return, though they did not say how or when.
options.note: Partly right about the return, but the angels specifically said He would come back the same way He left.

options.text: The disciples would see Jesus again only in visions and dreams.
options.note: This confuses His personal return with spiritual experiences; the promise is of a bodily, visible coming.

options.text: Jesus had gone for good and would not return.
options.note: The angels promised exactly the opposite: He will come back.

quiz.q: Why did Jesus say the disciples would receive power?

options.text: So that, filled with the Holy Spirit, they could be His witnesses.
options.note: The power of the Spirit is given for witness to Christ.

options.text: So that they could work miracles for their own reputation.
options.note: The power is for testifying to Jesus, not for personal glory.

options.text: So that they could carry out the mission Jesus gave them.
options.note: True in general, but the specific purpose named is to be His witnesses to the ends of the earth.

options.text: So that they could know the times and seasons the Father had fixed.
options.note: Jesus said such knowledge was not theirs to have; the power was for witness, not for calculating dates.

questions: Jesus told the apostles to wait for the Spirit before they went out. Where in your life are you tempted to serve God in your own strength rather than depending on His Spirit?

The disciples wanted to know times and seasons, but Jesus redirected them to their task. What questions about the future are you fixed on that God is gently turning back toward faithful obedience today?
You will be My witnesses. Who are the people, near and far, that God has placed within reach of your testimony to Jesus?
The angels asked why they stood gazing into the sky. Where might you be standing still, when Christ has given you work to do while you wait for Him?
This same Jesus will come back. How does the certainty of Christ's return shape the way you live and serve this week?

translationNotes.note: The phrase taken up to heaven translates the verb Luke uses for the ascension; some manuscripts vary slightly in wording, but the sense of Christ being received up is constant.
The phrase rendered while they were gathered together carries a footnote reading or eating together; either way it pictures the risen Jesus sharing table and instruction with the apostles.
Baptized with the Holy Spirit can also be rendered baptized in the Holy Spirit; the same promise is recalled in Acts 11:16.
